subsection: 3. The Irish in the USA and Britain: anti-Irish sentiment and political participation

notes.b: Famine-era emigrants were mostly poor, Catholic and unskilled, and they settled in the cities of the north-east USA and industrial Britain, where host communities saw them at close quarters. Hostility rested on religion, poverty and competition for work, and it was reinforced by stereotypes that were widely printed. This is discrimination: unfair treatment of a group in jobs, housing, politics or public life.
points: Religion: most Irish emigrants were Catholic, and Protestant Americans and Britons often saw Catholicism as foreign and a threat to their institutions, because they believed the Pope was a rival authority to the state.

Poverty and disease: the Irish who arrived in the Famine years were poor and crowded into slums, so outbreaks of cholera and typhus (diseases that spread easily in overcrowded, dirty housing) were blamed on them.

Crime and drink: Irish migrants were blamed for crime, drunkenness and disorder in the cities where they lived, and they were over-represented in arrest figures, which seemed to confirm the prejudice.
Competition for work: Irish labourers and servants competed with native-born and other workers, and their willingness to accept low wages created resentment among those who feared being undercut.
Racial stereotypes: the Irish were portrayed as a separate and inferior race, and in cartoons they were often drawn with apelike features, which made hostility seem natural rather than prejudiced.
Political fear: Protestants feared that Catholic voters would take orders from their priests, and that Irish nationalists would drag the host country into Irish quarrels.
notes.tip: For a Higher essay on anti-Irish sentiment, name the causes (religion, poverty and disease, competition for work, stereotypes) and give a dated example of each from both the USA and Britain. A list of causes without examples scores badly. For a short question on why emigrants were disliked, one cause with its reason is enough.

notes.h: Anti-Irish sentiment in the United States
notes.b: American nativism, the movement of native-born Protestants against immigrants and Catholic influence, was strongest in the 1840s and 1850s and went on in cartoons and job notices afterwards. In the USA it grew into a political party.
points: The Philadelphia riots of 1844 (May and July) were anti-Catholic disturbances in which nativist mobs attacked Irish Catholic homes and churches, after a dispute over which Bible, the Protestant King James Bible or the Catholic one, should be used in public schools.

Nativism became a political force, for example: the Know-Nothings, formally the American Party, won major state elections in 1854, including Massachusetts, their period of greatest strength, because many voters feared immigrant Catholic influence.
The Know-Nothings took their name from the secrecy of their members, who answered questions about the movement with 'I know nothing'.

They wanted longer residence before immigrants could become citizens and vote (a 21-year wait was a common demand) and wanted to keep Catholics and the foreign-born out of public office. The movement split over slavery in the mid-1850s and faded before the Civil War (1861).

'No Irish Need Apply' (NINA) was said to appear on job advertisements and signs in the 19th century. Richard Jensen argued in 2002 that written signs were rare and the memory exaggerated, while Rebecca Fried in 2015 found real newspaper advertisements, so historians disagree on how common they were.
Thomas Nast, in cartoons in Harper's Weekly in the 1870s, drew Irish Catholics, and Irish politicians especially, as ape-like and corrupt, which spread the stereotype to a mass audience.
Irish Americans responded by building their own parishes, schools, newspapers and societies, so they no longer depended on a hostile society, and by using the vote.
notes.tip: Do not state NINA signs as fact: examiners reward the debate between Jensen and Fried. Also keep the dates apart: the Know-Nothings are 1850s, Nast is 1870s. A strong answer notes that in the USA nativism became a political party.

notes.b: In Britain anti-Irish feeling was mixed with sectarian rivalry (hostility between Protestants and Catholics), and it flared at moments of Fenian threat. The Fenians were an Irish republican movement active in Ireland, Britain and America in the 1860s.
points: Punch magazine caricatured the Irish in the 1840s and 1860s, presenting them as simian (ape-like), violent and backward, so a respectable magazine helped to spread the stereotype.
The Stockport riots of June 1852 saw Irish Catholic homes and churches attacked in Stockport, Cheshire, after a Catholic procession in the town, which angered local Protestants.
The Murphy riots of 1867 followed the anti-Catholic lectures of William Murphy and brought attacks on Irish districts in English towns, chiefly Birmingham and also Wolverhampton.
In Liverpool and Glasgow, Protestant Orange lodges (societies of Protestants loyal to the Crown) and Catholic Irish communities clashed, so sectarian rivalry shaped local politics and street life.

Three Fenians, the Manchester Martyrs, were executed on 23 November 1867. Three weeks later, on 13 December 1867, a Fenian bomb at Clerkenwell prison in London killed about a dozen people, and fears grew that all Irish people in Britain were a security threat.
Fenian scares led to heavy policing of Irish districts, and Irish nationalists claimed that the state treated the whole community as suspect.
Writers blamed the Irish for typhus, low wages and crime in industrial towns, and the Victorian press often presented them as a separate race.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the Stockport riots (1852, after a Catholic procession) with the Murphy riots (1867, after anti-Catholic lectures), or the Manchester Martyrs (23 November 1867) with Clerkenwell (13 December 1867). A strong comparison says that in Britain hostility was mixed with sectarian rivalry and flared at Fenian threats.

notes.h: Irish political participation in the United States
notes.b: Irish Americans turned their numbers into political power through the Democratic Party and the city machines. To vote a migrant needed citizenship (naturalisation), and city government ran through patronage, meaning jobs and favours given in return for support, between two parties, Democrats and Republicans.
points: Most Irish Americans voted Democratic, because the party defended immigrants against nativist attacks and offered them jobs and help.
Ward politics: local party organisers in each ward (a district of a city) gave immigrants jobs, housing and legal help in return for votes, so the party became part of daily life.
Tammany Hall, the Democratic organisation in New York City, controlled city politics through patronage, jobs and contracts. John Kelly led it from 1872, the first Irish boss, after the Tweed era.
William R. Grace, born in Ireland, was elected mayor of New York in 1880, the first Irish-born Catholic mayor, and took office in 1881. Hugh O'Brien became mayor of Boston in 1885.
John F. Fitzgerald ('Honey Fitz', mayor 1906 to 1908 and 1910 to 1914) and James Michael Curley (mayor four times, first term from 1914) dominated Boston politics in the early 20th century.
Al Smith, a Catholic partly of Irish descent, was governor of New York in the 1920s and the Democratic presidential candidate in 1928, when he was defeated by Herbert Hoover.
Irish men were prominent in urban police forces and fire companies, and these jobs were a route into local politics because city jobs were handed out through the party.
Irish-American political success was built on group loyalty, so it gave immigrant communities a voice in city government.
notes.tip: Exams ask why Irish Americans voted Democratic: the party defended immigrants and gave jobs and help. For a paragraph, give a concrete example such as ward organisers giving jobs for votes. For a Higher essay, structure by country and end with a judgement on how much influence the Irish gained.

notes.b: Richard Croker turned Tammany Hall into the most powerful political machine in New York City, and his career shows both the opportunity and the corruption of machine politics.
points: Richard Croker was born in Co. Cork in 1843 and was taken to New York as a child, where he grew up in a poor Irish district.
He rose, for example, through the Fourth Avenue gang, the fire companies and the local Democratic clubs, and held minor city offices such as alderman and coroner.
He led Tammany Hall from the mid-1880s until 1902, using patronage, jobs in city departments and contracts to win support among immigrants and the poor.
He controlled Democratic nominations and so could place allies in office, including Robert Van Wyck, mayor of New York from 1898 to 1901.

The Lexow Committee (1894, a state inquiry into police corruption) and the Mazet Committee (1899, an inquiry into Tammany government) exposed the system. Tammany lost the mayoral election of 1901, and Croker left the leadership in 1902.
He retired to Ireland, where he lived at Glencairn near Dublin and bred racehorses; his horse Orby won the Epsom Derby in 1907.
Contemporary reformers and much of the respectable press condemned Croker's corruption, while many Tammany voters regarded him as a friend of the poor.

Historians now present him as the clearest example of machine politics, in which immigrant political success came with corruption, though they also see his career as a route of upward mobility for an immigrant.
notes.tip: Profiles need dated facts: birth, rise, Tammany leadership, Van Wyck, Lexow and Mazet, retirement and Orby. Do not confuse Lexow (1894, police) with Mazet (1899, city government), or Croker with John Kelly. Close with a judgement on what Croker shows about the Irish in America.

notes.b: Joseph P. Kennedy showed how an Irish American could rise to the top of business and then government, and his career was marked by controversy.
points: Joseph P. Kennedy was born in Boston in 1888, the son of Patrick J. Kennedy, a Boston politician and businessman, and he married Rose Fitzgerald, daughter of Mayor John F. Fitzgerald.
He built a fortune, for example, in banking, the stock market and the film industry before entering government.

He was the first chairman of the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) from 1934, a body set up to regulate the stock market after the crash of 1929, and he chaired the US Maritime Commission in 1937.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed him ambassador to Britain, 1938 to 1940, widely described as the first Irish Catholic in the post.

As ambassador he supported Neville Chamberlain's policy of appeasement (giving way to Germany to avoid war) and doubted that Britain could win a war with Germany. He resigned in late 1940 after an interview that was read as defeatist about Britain's chances.

Contemporary Irish-American opinion was divided because he was both a success story and a conservative: some were proud of his success, while others distrusted his conservative views and his closeness to the British government.
Historians judge him a self-made businessman and an appeaser whose pessimism ended his public career, and a father whose ambitions shaped his sons, including John F. Kennedy.
notes.tip: Learn the sequence of the SEC, the Maritime Commission and the ambassadorship with the resignation. Do not confuse Joseph P. Kennedy with his son John F. Kennedy, or with his own father Patrick J. Kennedy.

notes.b: Paul O'Dwyer combined a career as a New York lawyer with campaigns for civil rights and for Irish causes.
points: Paul O'Dwyer was born in Bohola, Co. Mayo, in 1907 and emigrated to New York in 1925, becoming a lawyer there in the 1930s. He was the brother of William O'Dwyer, mayor of New York from 1946 to 1950.
For example, he defended trade unionists and took on civil rights cases and causes for working people and immigrants, and he supported the civil rights movement.

He was a Democratic politician who was the party's candidate for the US Senate in 1968, opposed to the Vietnam War, and lost to Jacob Javits. He was president of the New York City Council from 1974 to 1977, in the mid-1970s.
He was active in Irish causes, and in later decades he supported civil rights for Catholics in Northern Ireland and criticised British policy there.
Contemporaries saw him as a liberal and a critic of the establishment, and because of this some thought his views on Northern Ireland too sympathetic to the republican cause.
Historians place him in the tradition of liberal Irish-American politics, in which civil rights and Irish nationalism were linked.
notes.tip: Remember the dated facts: Mayo birth, emigration in 1925, law, the 1968 Senate run and his brother William. Paul the lawyer is not William the mayor. Close with what he shows about the Irish in America.

notes.b: Irish people in Britain were British subjects after the Act of Union (1801), so they needed no naturalisation and their political voice took a different form from American machines. It worked through Irish nationalist organisation and then through Labour.
points: The Irish National League of Great Britain, founded in 1883, organised Irish voters behind the Irish Parliamentary Party, led by Charles Stewart Parnell.
In the general election of November and December 1885 Parnell told Irish voters in Britain to vote against the Liberals, which in effect meant voting Conservative.

T. P. O'Connor was elected MP for Liverpool Scotland in 1885 and held the seat until 1929, as a nationalist and a journalist. He is usually described as the only Irish nationalist elected for a British seat.
O'Connor founded newspapers in London, such as The Star (1888), and used the press to support Home Rule (self-government for Ireland) and Irish causes.

After Gladstone, the Liberal prime minister, introduced the first Home Rule Bill in 1886 (it was defeated), Irish voters in Liverpool and Glasgow largely supported the Liberal Party as the party of Home Rule.
From the early 20th century Irish voters in Britain increasingly backed the Labour Party, which also drew support from the working class.

Irish-born men could vote and stand for Parliament as British subjects, though the franchise was limited by property qualifications until the reforms of 1867 and 1884. This made participation easier than in the USA, where naturalisation was needed.
notes.tip: For Britain, structure the answer around the Irish National League of Great Britain, the 1885 and 1886 voting, T. P. O'Connor and Labour. The best answers explain why the forms differed: machines in the USA, the Parliamentary Party and Labour in Britain.

notes.b: The Molly Maguires were a secret society among Irish miners in the Pennsylvania anthracite (hard coal) coalfields, whose conflict with mine owners ended in executions.
points: The society operated in the anthracite coalfields of eastern Pennsylvania, especially Schuylkill County, in the 1860s and 1870s. It drew on the tradition of the Ribbonmen, an Irish agrarian secret society, and took the name of one.
Irish miners worked in dangerous conditions for low pay, which fed their grievances, and many members belonged to the Ancient Order of Hibernians, an Irish Catholic fraternal organisation.
Violence against mine bosses and police was blamed on the Mollies, so they were treated as a criminal conspiracy, who were accused of murders and arson.

Franklin B. Gowen, head of the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad and its coal company, hired the Pinkerton detective agency, and the detective James McParland infiltrated the society under the name James McKenna.

The Long Strike (December 1874 to June 1875) failed and broke the miners' union, the Workingmen's Benevolent Association. The trials of 1876 to 1878 followed, with convictions depending heavily on the evidence of informers and of McParland.

Twenty men were hanged between 1877 and 1879. Ten were hanged on a single day, 21 June 1877, known as the Day of the Rope, at Pottsville and Mauch Chunk, and the leader Jack Kehoe was hanged in December 1878.

Labour historians see the Mollies as victims of an employer-backed frame-up, while others see a real secret society using violence. Kevin Kenny (Making Sense of the Molly Maguires, 1998) argued they were a genuine society rooted in Irish agrarian violence, but that the trials were unfair.
Jack Kehoe was pardoned after his death, by the governor of Pennsylvania in 1979.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph give who and where, the conditions, Gowen and McParland, the trials, the hangings and one interpretation, each with a date. For Higher, name Kevin Kenny with his view; the Mollies as victims versus guilty is a paired judgement.

notes.b: Judgements on Irish political life in America and Britain turn on whether the Irish gained real influence despite discrimination, or only built machines and patronage. Assimilation, adopting the language, customs and habits of the new country, is the thread: political participation was one route to it.
points: Achievement: Irish politicians built lasting power in American cities and in some British seats, so they gave immigrants a route into public life.
Limit: machine politics relied on patronage and corruption, and reform movements challenged it from the 1880s onwards.

Success against discrimination: by the early 20th century Irish Americans were prominent in the police and city government, and Al Smith and Joseph Kennedy had reached national prominence, a sign that discrimination was being overcome.
Contemporary view: nativists and reformers condemned Irish politicians as corrupt, while Irish communities defended them as champions of immigrants.
Later view: historians disagree on whether Irish political success advanced assimilation or delayed it, because machine politics kept communities separate.
Britain versus the USA: the Irish in Britain had votes sooner, but their political voice was channelled into the Irish Parliamentary Party and Labour rather than into city machines.
notes.tip: Judgement points are rewarded as pairs: achievement against limit (power against corruption), contemporary against later view, and the Mollies as victims against guilty. Use politics and the police as the opportunity side and discrimination and the Molly Maguires as the challenge side.
